reader.title: False report of the lynching of Frank J. Wright
bases: A widely reprinted report that vigilantes lynched Wright and his servant in Colorado [A7, A3] was withdrawn when Wright telegraphed from Silver City, N.M., that he was alive [A22, A27].

The reports described a vigilance committee hanging Wright and his servant as mule thieves [A7, A6], but Wright was alive and telegraphed his father on Mar. 14, 1881 [A22, A27]; no report confirms that anyone was killed.
Many papers carried the lynching report from a single source, Dr. Wilson's letter [A7, A1], and later reports refuted it with Wright's own telegram [A22, A29, A23].

summary.text: The false report of the lynching of Frank J. Wright was a story, widely printed in March 1881, that Wright, a Washington, D.C., lawyer from Westminster, Maryland, had been killed in the Colorado mountains in 1880 by men who believed that mules in his possession were stolen.
Most versions said a "vigilance committee" hanged him and his servant despite their protests of innocence.
Two weeks later Wright telegraphed his father from Silver City, New Mexico, that he had read of his own death, and the papers withdrew the story.
Papers first treated it as the killing of an "innocent man" and then as "A Cruel Hoax."

According to the Westminster Democratic Advocate, Wright, a son of Isaac Wright of that city, left his Washington law practice for Colorado in May 1880 on a client's land claims and bought an interest in a gold mine.
His last letter, the Advocate said, was dated Ouray, Colorado, July 30, 1880.
When months passed without word, relatives asked the Rev. Dr. David Wilson, a former Westminster pastor serving as an army chaplain in Colorado, to inquire.
Wilson wrote back that in August Wright had bought mules and set out prospecting with a servant, that the mules proved stolen, and that a vigilance committee overtook and lynched the two men.

The first printed account, a Westminster dispatch to the Baltimore American reprinted in the Washington Evening Star on March 2, said the mules' owner and friends pursued Wright and "shot him dead, supposing that he was the thief."
A Baltimore wire of March 3 and 4 said instead that "a band of vigilants," also called "a gang of desperadoes," hanged Wright and his servant "before he could make an explanation."
A New York Herald version, credited to Wright's sister, Mrs. Gowen Spence of Newark, said the two were hanged "to the limb of a tree, where their skeletons were afterward found."
No account gave a place, a date or any names; the servant was called only "a Coloradoan."

The family's one ground for hope, a Westminster dispatch of March 15 said, had been a January letter from the postmaster at Hancock, Colorado, saying Wright had been there on November 11, after the supposed lynching.
On March 15 Isaac Wright received a telegram from Silver City, dated March 14: "Read to my horror an account of my death in the New York Herald. Arrived here after perilous adventure."
The family had sought government detectives to punish those responsible, but suspended the effort pending a letter from Wright.
The Wilmington Daily Republican reported "active measures" to learn how the false story began.
No later report explaining the "perilous adventure," the story's origin or the servant's fate was found.
The story spread by wire and exchange through early March, from Washington and New York to Memphis, Charlotte and Minnesota.
Headlines cast Wright as blameless: "An Innocent Man Lynched" in Wilmington and Charlotte, "Lynching an Innocent Man" in Rock Island, and "Lynched for No Cause" in Millheim, Pennsylvania.

Several papers turned it against lynch law: the Democratic Advocate called the vigilantes "a mob of outlaws" who held the theft of stock to be "the worst of crimes," and the Chicago Times account reprinted in Rock Island said they had "speedily vindicated law by murdering two innocent men."
The Clarke Courier of Berryville, Virginia, found no more painful illustration of the evil of lynch law.
Retractions followed from March 16 under headlines like "Not Lynched," "The Dead Alive" and "A Cruel Hoax."

Some papers still ran the original on March 17: the Millheim Journal printed the wire, and the Eureka Daily Sentinel printed the Herald version noting that morning's dispatches contradicted "the whole thing."
None of the papers stated the race of Wright or of his servant.
Before the retraction, the first dispatch said the mules' owner and friends shot Wright, while later versions said vigilantes hanged him with his servant.
His age was given as 27, 30 and 32.
The Daily Republican's retraction said it was the servant who had bought the animals.
Wright's telegram superseded all of these, though it said nothing of the servant.

framing.detail: Wire headlines 'An Innocent Man Lynched' and 'Horrible Work of a Band of Desperadoes'; 'The murder was a horrible one and wholly unprovoked.'
Hometown Democratic Advocate: 'innocent victims of a mob of outlaws' for whom stock theft is 'the worst of crimes'.
Chicago Times via Rock Island Argus: 'a most dastardly crime', vigilantes 'vindicated law by murdering two innocent men'.
Clarke Courier used the case to show 'the evil effect of lynch law'.
Retractions: 'Not Lynched', 'The Dead Alive', 'A Cruel Hoax'.

versions.value: Wright and servant lynched in Colorado

conflicts.note: The telegram from Wright himself, received by his father and reported by his hometown paper, is the better evidence; the Hancock postmaster's letter also placed him alive after the supposed lynching. No report on the servant after the retraction.
Only the Mar. 19 Daily Republican says the servant bought them.
July 30 is the date of his last letter in the hometown account.
